works.heading: Designing and building Still Here, a habit-reduction app
works.challenge: Most habit apps are built around a perfect streak, and they reset you to zero the second you slip. If you're reducing a habit instead of quitting it cold, that's basically a machine for feeling like a failure. I wanted the opposite: something that keeps every good day you've earned, forgives the days you don't, and never once shows you a red mark. And because it was mine, it had to be a real product, not a demo. Design, front end, backend, auth, domain, copy, and launch, all of it.
works.summary: Still Here is a habit app I designed and built on my own, start to finish. Instead of streaks and red X's, it turns any habit you're cutting back on into a small pixel-art island that grows a little every honest day. It's live at stillhere.day, free, no ads. This one's personal, so here's the whole thinking behind it.

sections.title: A forest that grows as you keep your oath.

sections.body: There was no client and no kickoff for this one. It started on a road trip to Halls Gap. Fresh air, a clean river, birds on the benches, and the first thing my brain offered up was "what a perfect spot to smoke." The only smoke around was coming from the meat shop. Everyone else was reading, eating ice cream, sipping coffee. For the first time I felt embarrassed by the thought. That day I made a small promise: enjoy the good things without a cigarette in my hand. Still Here is that promise turned into an app.

"What a perfect spot to smoke."
— The thought that started the whole thing.

sections.label: What I wanted to build:
items: A tracker for reducing a habit, not just quitting it
Something that grows when you do well, instead of punishing you when you don't

sections.label: What I refused to add:
items: Streaks that reset to zero
Red marks, shame, ads, or a subscription

sections.body: The promise was the easy part. The real question was how to build a habit app that doesn't quietly make you feel worse every time you open it. Everything after this was about answering that.

The whole product rests on one bet: make progress something you tend, not a number you have to protect. So every honest day plants something on your island, and it grows from bare soil to a seed, a sapling, a grove, and finally a haven full of animals at dusk. A second layer grows next to it, where little builders raise a home for each good day, from a bedroll up to a warm homestead with a fire going. Slip up and nothing gets torn down. The builders just rest by the fire until you're back.

sections.label: A few things I wanted to get right:
items: Blank days stay foggy, never red. A miss is missing data, not a punishment.
The app talks in your tone. You choose Gentle, Plain, or Honest, and the messages shift to match.
Rewards you can't rush. Companions and rare visitors (a butterfly, a rabbit, and if you keep at it, a unicorn or a little dragon) show up on their own as the forest matures.

sections.body: The pixel art and the cozy tone aren't just decoration, they're the actual argument. A place that feels alive is easier to come back to than a chart that's judging you.

Still Here is live at stillhere.day. It installs like a normal app since it's a PWA, runs from a single tap, and stays free with no ads and no subscription. Under the cozy surface it's a full build: the forest and homestead systems, the honest calendar, the tone engine, accounts and auth, the domain and email setup, and every word of copy. I did the thinking behind it, designed it, wrote it, built the front and back end, and shipped it.

That's the part I'd want a client to sit with. I can take something from a single thought on a park bench all the way to a live, installable product, by myself. Hand me a problem and I can own the whole thing: the research, the design, the code, the words, and the launch.

works.role: Solo. Research, design, build, copy, and launch.

works.heading: Turning a printed book into a playable public-space project
works.challenge: The book was never meant to sit still. It asks people to go out and do things: small actions, creative instructions, soft disruptions in the forgotten parts of their city. A printed copy can hold those assignments, but it can't hold what happens after someone actually does one. The challenge was to build the digital half of the book without flattening it into a normal website. It had to keep the book's quiet, playful, slightly strange feeling, let people play through it online, and give them a way to share what they made or noticed, so the project becomes something a whole city can add to, not just read.
works.summary: Let This Book Be Your Public Space is Jody Agus's book about public space in Jakarta, a city where there's very little of it. It's part game, part toolkit, part poetic ritual: instead of being read, it wants to be used. I worked with Jody to shape, design, and build the website that turns the printed book into something interactive, where people can play the book online and share what they did with its assignments. It was made for Jody's exhibition at the Locarno Film Festival's BaseCamp program.
works.time: TBD — confirm number of weeks · Made for Locarno Film Festival's BaseCamp program, 2025

sections.title: A book that wants to be used, not read.

sections.body: This one started as a conversation between me and Jody about a book that refused to behave like a book. He'd made something you're supposed to enter, wander through, and gently abandon, built for a city where public space is scarce but imagination isn't. My part was figuring out how the web could carry that same spirit instead of turning it into a product page.

"The book doesn't want to be read. It wants to be used. I need the website to feel the same way, like a space you step into, not a thing you scroll."
— Jody Agus

sections.label: What are we building?
items: A digital version of the book people can play through online
A way for people to share their responses to the book's assignments
A site that holds the book's tone, not just its text

sections.label: What are the goals?
items: Extend the printed book into something interactive
Let readers become participants, and see each other's activities
Give the Locarno exhibition a living, online companion

sections.body: The trap with a project like this is building a clean, normal website that quietly kills the whole idea. Jody's book is strange on purpose. So before anything else, we spent time on tone: how the site should feel to move through, and how playing the book online could feel as open-ended as doing it in the street.

Because the book is the concept, most of the work was translation: taking something made of paper, characters, and quests, and deciding what each part becomes on a screen. I worked closely with Jody on that, so the site reads as an extension of his book rather than my interpretation of it.

sections.label: The parts that took the most thought:
items: Playing the book online. The characters each offer a lens on public space, and each comes with quests, small actions and creative instructions. The site had to make those playable, not just readable.
Sharing back. The book asks you to do things in the real world, so people needed a way to post what they did, turning solo assignments into something a community builds together.
Holding the tone. Poetic, a little unfinished, meant to be wandered and abandoned. Every design and build decision came back to protecting that feeling.

sections.body: This wasn't a case of a client handing over a brief and stepping back. It was shaping an artist's idea into a working thing alongside him, which is a different skill than just building to spec, and honestly the part I like most.

What we made is the book's second half. People can move through it online, play the characters and their quests, and share what they did with the assignments, so the project keeps growing past the printed copy. It went out into the world through Jody's exhibition at Locarno's BaseCamp program in 2025, and online it stays open for anyone in Jakarta, or anywhere, to add to.

That's the note I'd want a client to sit with. Give me something conceptual, even something that resists being a normal website, and I can work with you to shape it, design it, and build it into something real that people actually use. Not every brief is a shop or a landing page. Some are ideas that need a collaborator to make them work on the web, and that's work I'm built for.

works.heading: Building a booking store for a travel agency
works.challenge: Selling a trip isn't like selling a t-shirt. A product has a size and a price. A trip has departure dates, a deposit or a full payment, a capacity, and a schedule that repeats. Shopify is built for physical products, so the real work was making it behave like a booking system without losing the smooth checkout Shopify is good at. On top of that, Klana's whole appeal is feeling adventurous and personal, so the site had to carry that mood and still handle the unglamorous mechanics of taking someone's money for a specific date.
works.summary: Klana is a Jakarta travel agency that runs curated trips: open trips, treks, culinary experiences, and its own "blind trip" where the destination is a surprise. My client needed a site where people could browse those trips and actually book and pay, not just read a brochure. I built it on Shopify and bent it to fit how trips work, with departure dates, deposit options, and open-trip scheduling. It's live and taking bookings at klana.co.id. Here's how it works underneath.
works.time: TBD — confirm number of weeks · Built with Shopify, plus a local payment app (confirm which)

sections.title: Experience the magic of the unknown.

sections.body: Klana came in with trips already running and a clear personality, but no proper way to sell online. They wanted people to be able to find a trip, pick a date, and pay, all in one place, without it turning into a back-and-forth over chat every time.

"We run real trips with real dates and limited spots. The site can't just be a catalogue, people need to book and pay on it. But it still has to feel like Klana, like an adventure, not a booking form."
— Klana

sections.label: What are we building?
items: A Shopify store where people browse and book trips
Date-based booking with deposit or full-payment options
A site that feels like the trips, not a spreadsheet

sections.label: What are the goals?
items: Let customers book and pay online, end to end
Handle open trips, upcoming trips, and trip categories cleanly
Keep Klana's adventurous, personal tone throughout

sections.body: The interesting problem here was fitting a booking model into a shop platform. Before building anything, I mapped how Klana's trips actually work, the dates, the deposits, the repeat departures, because that structure had to drive the whole store, not the other way around.

Most of the work was making Shopify think in trips instead of products. Each trip carries its own set of departure dates, a full-payment or deposit choice, and a price, and the store is organized so people can browse by what they want: special trips, upcoming trips, and categories like outdoor, water, road trip, and eco.

sections.label: The parts that took the most thought:
items: Trips as bookable products. Departure dates, deposit vs full payment, and capacity, all handled through the product and checkout so a "trip" behaves like a booking, not a one-off item.
Local payment. I integrated a local payment gateway through third-party apps, so customers pay the way they already pay here, including the deposit option for bigger trips.
Browsing that matches how people choose. Sorting trips into special, upcoming, and clear categories, so someone can come in wanting "a water adventure" and land on the right thing fast.

sections.body: The deposit-versus-full-payment piece matters more than it looks. A big trip is a real spend, and letting people commit with a deposit lowers the barrier to booking. That's a business decision the store had to support, not just a checkout setting.

klana.co.id is live and taking bookings. People browse trips by category, pick a departure date, choose to pay a deposit or in full, and check out through local payment. It handles open trips, upcoming departures, and Klana's signature blind trip, and it carries the brand's adventurous tone the whole way through, from the "magic of the unknown" hero down to the trip pages.

For anyone deciding whether to hire me, here's the useful part. This wasn't a standard store. It's a booking system living inside Shopify, with dates, deposits, and local payment all working together. I can take a business model that doesn't fit the platform out of the box and make the platform serve it, cleanly enough that customers just see a site that works.

works.title: klana.co.id

works.heading: Design and Shopify development for a two-market fashion brand
works.challenge: Running two markets means running two sets of expectations: different payment methods, different shipping partners, different currencies, but one brand. The build had to keep both storefronts feeling like a single label while giving the team enough flexibility in Shopify to manage editorial content and pricing without needing a developer for every change.
works.summary: quietundernone.com is a fashion brand selling across Indonesian and international markets. I've handled design and Shopify development for them — from custom collection templates to local payment and shipping integrations — as they've grown into a two-storefront operation. Here's a look at that work.

sections.body: I built custom Shopify collection page templates powered by metafields, so editorial content can be swapped in without touching theme code. On the backend, I'm migrating payment gateways from Midtrans to Xendit and working toward unifying the Indonesian and international stores under Shopify Markets, so the team can manage one catalog instead of two.

works.title: quietundernone.com

works.heading: Designing and building a single-page luxury fashion drop site
works.challenge: A single-shirt drop needs to feel like an event, not a product page. The brief was to make one shirt feel worth the wait — full-screen presentation, real texture and detail, sound, motion — and since there's a new drop every season, it also had to run without a developer in the loop. Updating stock, images, or copy couldn't mean opening a code editor.
works.summary: SANTAI is a luxury fashion label built around a seasonal drop model — one exclusive shirt released per season. I designed and built the entire site as a single immersive page, with a password-protected CMS built in, so the brand can launch new drops and update pricing, images, and sizing without touching code. Here's how it came together.

sections.body: Built as a single HTML file backed by Supabase for data and storage: a full-screen shirt display with 360° drag-to-rotate and front/back swap, a hold-to-reveal detail panel with looping audio, swipe navigation between drops, and a password-protected CMS covering everything from the logo and background to each article's copy, images, and availability. Client-side image compression and localStorage caching keep it fast without a heavy stack.

works.heading: Creating a digital radio station and landing page
works.challenge: Antasiar had a strong identity but no home online. The job was to turn a loud, retro brand into a site people could actually use: press play and listen, find the shows, meet the hosts, grab merch. All of that without sanding off the personality that makes it feel like Antasiar. It also had to ship fast and run on WordPress so the team could keep it updated themselves.
works.summary: Antasiar is an online radio brand built around a station that was big in the 80s and had gone quiet by the 90s. In 2024 it came back, and this site is where it lives: a live player, the shows, the voices behind the mic, and the merch. I designed and built the whole thing in WordPress. Here's how it came together.

sections.body: Good projects tend to start over coffee, and ours was no different. We sat down, ordered, and talked through what Antasiar actually needed to be online.

"We've already done the market research. What I want is a site that sounds like us: loud, a little nostalgic, fun to click around, and I want it live soon."
— Client

sections.label: What are we building?
items: A landing page
A live streaming player (the radio itself)

sections.label: What are the goals?
items: A site that tells people who Antasiar is
Analytics, so the team can see who's actually listening

sections.body: First meeting done, direction set. Most of it was about the audience: who tunes into an indie-leaning online radio, and how a site pulls them in and keeps them there. Before I touched a single layout, I wanted to test my assumptions instead of guessing. Stay with me, this is the part I like.

The brand is loud, but the site still has to be easy to move around. So before wireframing, I ran a card sort to see where people expect to find things. The point was to build the menu around their mental model, not ours.

sections.label: What we wanted to discover:
items: Where people look first for the live player
How they expect to browse the shows
Where they'd go to read Antasiar's story
Where they'd look for the hosts (the juru siar)
Where they'd expect merch to live
What would actually make them follow on Spotify, Instagram, or YouTube

sections.caption: Cards used in the sort: main menu, sub-menu, and features.

sections.body: [N] people took part, run through an online card-sorting tool so gathering it was quick. I can't share the full breakdown here, but it settled a couple of real debates, mainly the menu order and where the player should sit on the page.

Antasiar's audience skews young, and that shaped most of the visual calls. Gen-z listeners are used to sites that feel alive and react when you touch them, so a flat, safe layout would have read as off-brand before anyone pressed play.

The palette leans warm and loud on purpose. Reds against a cream base, with sharp accent blocks that carry energy without feeling corporate. It reads as playful and current, and it doesn't lock into any one gender, which fits where the brand and its audience are heading.

What we shipped is a WordPress site the Vindes team can run on their own. Live player up top, the shows laid out clearly, Iqbaal front and center as the face of it, merch one click away, and every social handle wired in. Designed, built, and live in two weeks.

works.heading: Creating a website and content system for a national cycling federation
works.challenge: A national federation has a lot to keep online and a small team to keep it there. Race schedules change, news comes in weekly, new regulations get published, riders need to register for licenses, and all of it has to work in both Indonesian and English. They needed one site that could hold all of that and still look the part for a national sport, plus a back end the staff could run without a developer on call.
works.summary: The Indonesian Cycling Federation (ICF) is the national governing body for cycle racing in Indonesia. It needed one place online for everything it runs: races, news, rider licenses, regulations, the gallery, and its own history. I built the site as a React front end backed by Strapi, so the team can publish and update all of it without touching code. Here's how it came together.

sections.body: Good projects tend to start over coffee, and this one did too. We sat down with the ISSI team and mapped out everything the federation needed online, and who it was really for.

"We're the national body, so the site has to carry that weight. But we're also updating things constantly, races, news, licenses, and we can't wait on a developer every time. Make it look serious, and make it ours to run."
— Client

sections.label: What are we building?
items: A public website (news, events, disciplines, gallery, history)
A content system the team manages themselves (Strapi)
Rider license registration and regulations, in two languages

sections.label: What are the goals?
items: A credible home for the national federation
A back end the staff can update without code
Content that works in both Indonesian and English

sections.body: First meeting done, scope clear. The hard part was never any single page. It was that the federation publishes all the time and the team is small, so the site had to be built around how they actually work. Before drawing a single screen, I spent time on that, and on how other national federations organize the same kinds of content. Stay with me, this is where it gets useful.

A federation site lives or dies on findability. There's a lot here, and people arrive with very different goals: a rider wants a license, a fan wants results, an organizer wants regulations. So before wireframing, I mapped every content type and ran a card sort to check that the menu matched where people expected things to be, not just how the org is structured internally.

sections.label: What we wanted to discover:
items: Where riders go to register for a license
How people expect to find race schedules and results
Where they look for regulations
How fans browse news and the gallery
Where the federation's history and "about" belong
What the staff need to publish and update most often

sections.caption: Cards used in the sort: main menu, sub-menu, and content types.

sections.body: [N] people took part, a mix of riders and federation staff, run through an online card-sorting tool so it was quick to gather. I can't share the full results here, but it did two things: it reshaped the public menu, and it told me how to structure Strapi so the team publishes the way they already think, instead of learning a system built for a developer.

ISSI's audience is broad. Competitive riders chasing licenses and results, casual cyclists reading the news, event organizers, and the staff running the whole thing day to day. The site had to feel official enough to represent the sport nationally, without turning into a stiff government page nobody wants to visit.

The look leans dark and high-contrast, with red accents and full-bleed race photography doing most of the work. It reads as serious and current, and it keeps the riders and the racing up front, which is the whole point of a federation site.

What we shipped is a React site backed by Strapi that the ISSI team runs on their own. News, events, disciplines, gallery, and regulations all publish from the CMS in both languages, and the race hub and live indicator keep the front page current during events. I built it, but the point was to hand it over. The federation runs it now without me.
